label: Determinants as the Computational Heart
notes: This chapter, printed pages 93 to 108, reframes the determinant from a coordinate expansion into a first-class geometric object. Tell students that almost every incidence theorem in the book will be re-expressed as a vanishing bracket, so mastering brackets now pays off across the entire course.

label: Three Defining Properties
notes: Stress that multilinearity, the alternating property, and normalization pin the determinant down uniquely. Every later identity follows from these three axioms alone, so when a sign flips or a term cancels, point back to which axiom is doing the work rather than to a coordinate computation.

label: Oriented Area and Volume
notes: Connect the alternating axiom to geometry: the determinant measures signed area in the plane and signed volume in space. The sign is orientation, and a zero value is degeneracy. Have students predict the sign before computing so the geometry leads the algebra.

label: The Bracket of Three Points
notes: Introduce bracket notation as the determinant of three homogeneous column vectors. Emphasize it is twice the signed triangle area in the affine chart with last coordinate one. This single scalar simultaneously records area magnitude, orientation, and the degeneracy we care about most.

label: Collinearity as a Vanishing Bracket
notes: Walk through the central equivalence: the bracket of three points is zero exactly when they are collinear. Use the sweep figure to show the bracket passing through zero and flipping sign as a point crosses the line, behaving like a signed distance proxy.

label: Duality: Concurrent Lines
notes: Point out that the bracket statement dualizes verbatim: three lines are concurrent exactly when the determinant of their coefficient vectors vanishes. Remind students that in the projective plane points and lines are interchangeable, so every bracket theorem comes with a free dual partner.

label: Cross Product and Cramer's Rule
notes: Show that join and meet are cross products and that the bracket is the triple product dotting one point against the cross product of the other two. Cramer's rule then reads each coordinate as a ratio of brackets, so solving linear systems becomes pure bracket bookkeeping.

label: Plucker's Mu Construction
notes: Explain Plucker's mu as a recipe: combine two equations so their shared zeros survive while a new point is forced. Evaluating each line at the target supplies the coefficients. This turns the abstract pencil of lines into a concrete construction students can compute by hand.

label: Brackets Build Invariants
notes: Make the invariance argument concrete: a projective map multiplies every three-bracket by the determinant of the transformation, and rescaling a point multiplies its brackets by that scale. A multihomogeneous polynomial is engineered so every term inherits the identical nonzero factor, leaving its zero set fixed.

label: Grassmann-Plucker Relations
notes: Present the Grassmann-Plucker relations as universal syzygies among brackets that vanish for every configuration. They are algebraic identities, not special cases, and they explain why different looking bracket formulas can certify the same incidence theorem behind the scenes.

label: A Relation Certifies an Incidence
notes: Use the area-cancellation figure to make the four-term relation tangible: four oriented triangle areas sum to zero identically. Then show how splitting the identity rearranges into the concurrency condition, so the syzygy is literally the proof that three constructed lines meet.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Close by collecting the through-line: brackets name determinants at the right altitude, collinearity and concurrence are bracket zeros, Plucker's mu constructs, multihomogeneity gives invariance, and Grassmann-Plucker relations are the engine behind incidence proofs. Preview that later chapters compute almost entirely in this bracket algebra.
